question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Today she said to her friend, “You're the sweetest person I have met ever”.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I have met ever”.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence uses the fixed structure for a superlative statement with the Present Perfect tense: Superlative adjective + Noun + (that) + Subject + have/has + ever + V3.

• In this pattern, the adverb "ever" must be placed before the past participle (V3), not after it. The correct order is "I have ever met", not "I have met ever".

◦ Example: She is the kindest person I have ever known. (not "I have known ever")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "her friend, “You're" — correct as printed; introduces the quoted speech correctly with a comma and opening quotation mark.

• Option 3: "Today she said to" — correct as printed; correctly introduces the reported/direct speech in the past tense ("said").

• Option 4: "the sweetest person" — correct as printed; the superlative form "the sweetest" is correctly used with the definite article "the".

NOTE

• The word "ever" in such superlative sentences always sits immediately before the main verb in its perfect form: "the best film I have ever seen", "the worst day I have ever had".

• Do not confuse this with simple questions like "Have you ever met him?", where "ever" also precedes the verb but the sentence is interrogative, not a superlative statement.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an INCORRECT preposition.
Please remember to take / your notice to the reception area / if you want it to be displayed / upon the bulletin board.
option_3: if you want it to be displayed
option_4: your notice to the reception area
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. upon the bulletin board.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct preposition to indicate something fixed or displayed on a flat surface (a board, wall, table, etc.) is "on", not "upon".

• Rule: "Upon" is generally used to indicate movement onto a surface or in fixed/formal expressions (e.g., "upon arrival", "upon request", "jump upon the table"), whereas "on" is used for a static position on a surface, such as a notice fixed on a board.

◦ Example: The notice is displayed on the bulletin board. (not "upon the bulletin board")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Please remember to take" is correct; "remember to + V1" is the correct structure for a future reminder.

• Option 3: "if you want it to be displayed" is correct; the passive infinitive "to be displayed" is correctly used after "want it".

• Option 4: "your notice to the reception area" is correct; the preposition "to" correctly shows direction/destination ("take something to a place").

NOTE

• Common preposition confusions tested by SSC: "on/upon/onto", "in/into", "between/among", "besides/beside".

• "On" is generally used with static, everyday surfaces (on the wall, on the board, on the table); "upon" suits more abstract/formal contexts (upon reflection, upon his return).

question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with a grammatical error.
The class / teacher was / wounded in / a leg.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. a leg.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• When referring to an injury to a specific part of one's own body, English idiom requires the definite article "the", not the indefinite article "a/an", before the body part.

• Rule: Subject + was/were + wounded/injured/hit/shot + in/on + the + body part.

◦ Example: The soldier was wounded in the leg. (not "a leg")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "teacher was" is grammatically correct; the singular subject "teacher" correctly takes the singular auxiliary "was".

• Option 3: "wounded in" is correct; "wounded" correctly takes the preposition "in" before a body part.

• Option 4: "The class" is correct; "The class teacher" is a correctly formed noun phrase.

NOTE

• The same rule applies to other similar expressions: "shot in the arm", "hit on the head", "injured in the knee" — always with "the", never "a/an", when referring to one's own body part.

question:
The following sentence has been divided into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Don't go / outside / because it is / raining heavy.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. raining heavy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A verb must be modified by an adverb, not an adjective. Here, the verb "raining" needs the adverb "heavily", not the adjective "heavy".

• Rule: Adjectives modify nouns/pronouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Most adverbs of manner are formed by adding "-ly" to the adjective (heavy → heavily).

◦ Example: It is raining heavily outside. (not "raining heavy")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Don't go" is correct; the negative imperative is correctly formed with "Don't + V1".

• Option 2: "outside" is correct; it is correctly used as an adverb of place here.

• Option 4: "because it is" is correct; "because" correctly introduces the reason/cause clause.

NOTE

• Similarly confused adjective/adverb pairs often tested by SSC: "hard/hardly", "late/lately", "near/nearly", "high/highly" — each pair has different meanings and uses.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The tuatara, which lives on New Zealand's islands, is affectionately known as Living fossil. It is called that because it is the only (1)_____ reptile in a group of reptiles that dates back about 220 million years to the time of the dinosaurs. The colour of the tuatara is grey or olive green. It (2)______ to a length of around 60 cm. The fact that this lizard has three eyes is its most (3)_______ feature. The pineal eye is the name given to the cone-shaped third eye. This eye is in a space between the brain and head. It has an eyelid over the third eye, which closes on a horizontal level. The tuatara has teeth that are (4)_______ from those of other reptiles. The lower jaw has only one row of teeth, while the upper jaw has two rows.

The tuatara is most active at night. It eats the eggs of birds, frogs, rats and insects. A tuatara's average lifespan is less than 77 years, but some species can live up to 100 years. In the spring, the female tuatara lays 8 to 15 eggs. These eggs are (5)______ during summer.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. living.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that shows the tuatara is the only surviving member of an ancient reptile group that otherwise died out (went extinct). "Living" correctly conveys that it is the sole species of that group that is still alive today.

• This matches the passage's opening idea that the tuatara is called a "Living fossil" — a still-existing species that resembles creatures known mainly from fossils.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "being" is grammatically odd here and does not convey the sense of "still surviving"; it does not fit naturally as an adjective before "reptile".

• Option 3: "entity" is a noun, not an adjective, so it cannot be used to modify "reptile" in this position.

• Option 4: "life" is also a noun and cannot grammatically modify "reptile" here; it does not fit the sentence structure.

NOTE

• Cloze passages test both grammatical fit (part of speech) and contextual/meaning fit — always check that the chosen word matches the surrounding sentence in both respects.

• The phrase "Living fossil" refers to a living species that closely resembles organisms otherwise known only from the fossil record, such as the coelacanth and the tuatara.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. develops.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes the tuatara's gradual physical growth to its adult size. "Develops" correctly conveys the sense of growing over time to reach a length of around 60 cm.

• The verb "develop" is commonly used to describe an organism's growth or maturation process, matching the passage's description of the animal's size.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "creates" means "to make or produce something new"; it does not fit the idea of an animal growing to a certain size.

• Option 3: "links" means "to connect"; it makes no logical sense in the context of an animal's growth to a length.

• Option 4: "nourishes" means "to provide with food/nutrients"; it does not describe growth to a physical length.

NOTE

• Commonly confused verbs of growth/change tested by SSC: "develop" (grow/mature), "evolve" (change gradually over generations), "expand" (increase in size/extent), "grow" (increase naturally in size).

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. intriguing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank needs a word meaning "fascinating" or "arousing great interest or curiosity", to describe the unusual fact that the tuatara has three eyes. "Intriguing" fits this meaning exactly.

• Intriguing = capturing one's attention or curiosity because it is unusual or mysterious.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "absorbing" means "holding one's complete attention", but it is typically used for activities (an absorbing book/game), not for a physical "feature" of an animal.

• Option 3: "diverting" means "entertaining or amusing", which does not suit the description of a biological feature.

• Option 4: "escalating" means "increasing rapidly", which is unrelated to describing an interesting feature.

NOTE

• Words meaning "fascinating/interesting" often tested by SSC: intriguing, captivating, absorbing, engrossing, fascinating — note their subtle differences in usage (people/things vs activities).

The colour of the tuatara is grey or olive green. It (2)______ to a length of around 60 cm. The fact that this lizard has three eyes is its most (3)_______ feature. The pineal eye is the name given to the cone-shaped third eye. This eye is in a space between the brain and head. It has an eyelid over the third eye, which closes on a horizontal level. The tuatara has teeth that are (4)_______ from those of other reptiles. The lower jaw has only one row of teeth, while the upper jaw has two rows.

The tuatara is most active at night. It eats the eggs of birds, frogs, rats and insects. A tuatara's average lifespan is less than 77 years, but some species can live up to 100 years. In the spring, the female tuatara lays 8 to 15 eggs. These eggs are (5)______ during summer.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. distinct.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by the preposition "from", and the standard collocation in English is "distinct from", meaning "different from" or "not the same as".

• Rule — Fixed collocation: "Distinct" pairs with "from" (distinct from), just as "different" also pairs with "from" (different from).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "separate" does not idiomatically collocate with "from" in this sense of "different in kind"; "separate from" usually means physically apart, not "different in kind".

• Option 3: "discrete" means "individually distinct/separate" but does not naturally collocate with "from" in this comparative sense; it also risks confusion with "discreet".

• Option 4: "sharp" describes the physical quality of teeth (pointed), not how they compare with other reptiles' teeth, and does not collocate with "from".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "discrete" (separate, individually distinct) with "discreet" (careful/tactful in speech or behaviour) — a common SSC spelling-cum-vocabulary trap.

• Other fixed preposition collocations: different from, similar to, identical to/with, independent of.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. fertilised.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Among the four options, only "fertilised" is the term appropriate for describing a process related to eggs. The others are terms specific to plants, not animal eggs.

• Fertilised = an egg that has been made capable of developing into a new organism, which is the biologically correct term to use for eggs.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "pollinated" refers to the transfer of pollen in flowering plants, not to animal eggs.

• Option 3: "germinated" refers to a seed beginning to grow/sprout, again a plant-related process, not applicable to eggs.

• Option 4: "fructified" means "to bear fruit" or "to produce results", a term used for plants/abstract outcomes, not for animal eggs.

NOTE

• Commonly confused biological process words tested by SSC: pollinated (flowers), germinated (seeds), fertilised (eggs/ova), fructified (fruit-bearing/figurative "to bear results").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Around the clock
option_1: Something that is done at night
option_2: Something that is done within one hour
option_4: Something that goes on day and night
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Something that goes on day and night.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Around the clock" means continuously, all day and all night, without stopping. (चौबीसों घंटे/दिन-रात)

◦ Example: The hospital staff worked around the clock to save the accident victims.

• The image behind the idiom is of the hands of a clock moving continuously through all 24 hours, symbolising non-stop activity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Something that is done at night — incorrect; the idiom does not refer only to night-time activity, but to continuous activity through both day and night.

• Option 2: Something that is done within one hour — incorrect; this describes speed/duration of one hour, not continuous round-the-clock activity.

• Option 3: Something that is time bound — incorrect; "time bound" means having a fixed deadline, which is the opposite sense of continuous, unending activity.

NOTE

• Other time-related idioms often asked in SSC: "In the nick of time" (just in time), "Once in a blue moon" (very rarely), "Time and again" (repeatedly).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Best thing since sliced bread
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Extremely good, interesting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "The best thing since sliced bread" is used to describe something (or someone) considered to be an excellent innovation or a truly wonderful, remarkable thing. (बहुत ही उत्कृष्ट/शानदार चीज़)

◦ Example: According to my grandmother, the smartphone is the best thing since sliced bread.

• The idiom originates from the introduction of pre-sliced packaged bread in the early 20th century, which was seen as a very convenient innovation at the time.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Breaking news (ताज़ा खबर): Refers to a current, urgent news story — unrelated to this idiom's meaning of "excellent/innovative".

• Option 2: Something to be cautious about (सावधान रहने योग्य बात): This is the opposite sense; the idiom expresses praise, not caution.

• Option 4: Rated well amongst cooks: A literal, narrow misreading connected to "bread"; the idiom is general praise, not restricted to cooking or chefs.

NOTE

• Similar idioms of high praise often tested by SSC: "A cut above the rest" (better than others), "Second to none" (the very best), "The cream of the crop" (the best of a group).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Ablaze
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Burning.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ablaze" means on fire, burning fiercely, or figuratively, brightly lit up or full of strong emotion. (जलता हुआ/प्रज्वलित)

◦ Example: The old warehouse was soon ablaze after the electrical short circuit.

• As a synonym, "Burning" correctly captures the literal sense of being on fire.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Extinguished" (बुझा हुआ): Means the exact opposite of "ablaze" — a fire that has been put out.

• Option 3: "Brazen" (ढीठ/निर्लज्ज): Means bold and shameless, unrelated in meaning to "on fire".

• Option 4: "Sharp" (तेज़): Means having a fine edge or being quick-witted; unrelated to the meaning of "ablaze".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "ablaze": aflame, ignited, alight, flaming.

• Figurative use: "Her eyes were ablaze with anger" — meaning full of intense emotion, not literal fire.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Mr. Stein is a very cold and hard man.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Charitable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the given sentence, "hard" means unfeeling, harsh, strict, or lacking kindness/sympathy towards others. (कठोर/निर्दयी)

• Its antonym should convey being generous, kind-hearted, and sympathetic towards others. "Charitable" means generous and kind in giving help, or forgiving/lenient in judging others, which is the opposite of being "hard" or unfeeling. (उदार/दयालु)

◦ Example: Unlike her hard-hearted brother, she is a charitable and warm-hearted woman.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Clement" (नरम/दयालु): Means "mild" (of weather) or "merciful/lenient" (of a person, especially in judgment); it is a near-synonym in a narrower legal/formal sense but does not capture general kindness of character as precisely as "charitable" does.

• Option 2: "Relaxed" (शिथिल/आरामदेह): Means calm and free from tension; it describes a state of mind, not kindness of character, so it is not a true antonym of "hard" in this sense.

• Option 4: "Tolerant" (सहिष्णु): Means willing to accept behaviour/opinions one disagrees with; it relates to open-mindedness, not specifically to kindness or generosity of nature.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "hard" (of a person): harsh, stern, callous, unfeeling, ruthless.

• Other antonyms of "hard" (of a person): kind, gentle, compassionate, tender-hearted, benevolent.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Many developing nations are having a ___________ economy these days.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. booming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a word that collocates with "economy" to mean rapidly growing, thriving, or prosperous. "Booming" is the standard collocation used for a fast-growing economy.

• Rule — Fixed collocation: "a booming economy" = an economy that is growing very quickly and successfully.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "boosting" means "increasing/promoting something"; it is typically used as a transitive verb (to boost the economy), not as an adjective directly describing "economy" in this way.

• Option 2: "resounding" means "loud and clear" or, figuratively, "emphatic" (a resounding victory); it does not collocate with "economy".

• Option 3: "ringing" literally means "making a bell-like sound"; figuratively it can mean "emphatic" (a ringing endorsement), but it does not collocate with "economy".

NOTE

• Common economy-related collocations tested by SSC: a booming economy, a sluggish economy, a stagnant economy, a robust economy, a fragile economy.

question:
Read the sentence carefully and select the synonym of the underlined word from the given alternatives.
Everyone revered my austere father who was the high priest of the famous Shiva temple.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Stern.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Austere" means strict, serious, and self-disciplined in manner; showing no luxury or excess. (कठोर/सादा)

• "Stern" means serious, strict, and uncompromising in manner, which closely matches the meaning of "austere" as used to describe a person's demeanour. (कठोर/गंभीर)

◦ Example: The austere/stern high priest allowed no frivolity during the temple rituals.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Composed" (शांत/संयत): Means calm and in control of one's emotions; it does not carry the sense of strictness or severity that "austere" conveys.

• Option 3: "Morose" (उदास/चिड़चिड़ा): Means sullen, gloomy, and ill-tempered; it describes a bad mood, not strictness or simplicity of manner.

• Option 4: "Aged" (वृद्ध): Simply means old in age; it has no connection to strictness or self-discipline.

NOTE

• "Austere" can also describe a simple, plain lifestyle without luxury, e.g., "an austere room with no decoration."

• Other synonyms of "austere": strict, severe, ascetic, rigorous, unadorned.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient to make me an English teacher.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. The little.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct idiomatic structure is "The little that + Subject + Verb...", meaning "the small amount that...". The definite article "The" is required before "little" when it refers to a specific, limited quantity being discussed.

• Rule: "The little" + relative clause (that/which) is used to mean "the small amount of something (that exists)", e.g., "The little he earns is spent on rent."

◦ Example: The little that I knew of the English language was not sufficient to make me an English teacher.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "So little" would imply "such a small amount", but does not fit the relative clause structure "...that I knew..." grammatically in this sentence as a subject.

• Option 2: "A little" means "a small amount" but is normally used without a following restrictive relative clause defining it as here; it does not fit this specific idiomatic pattern.

• Option 4: "Very little" emphasises smallness ("hardly any") but, like "a little", does not fit the definite, specific sense required by the relative clause "that I knew" as naturally as "the little" does.

NOTE

• Compare: "little" (almost no/hardly any — negative sense), "a little" (a small amount — positive sense), "the little" (the small amount that exists, often used with a defining relative clause).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
My most vivid recollection of that summer is the ocean.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Vague.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Vivid" means producing powerful, clear, and detailed images in the mind; strikingly clear. (स्पष्ट/जीवंत)

• "Vague" means not clear or precise in meaning or thought; indistinct, which is the direct opposite of "vivid". (अस्पष्ट)

◦ Example: My memory of that day is vague, unlike my vivid memory of my wedding day.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Eloquent" (वाक्पटु): Means fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing; it describes speech, not clarity of memory/image, so it is unrelated as an antonym.

• Option 3: "Pictorial" (सचित्र): Means relating to or expressed in pictures; it is actually closer in sense to "vivid" (image-like) rather than being its opposite.

• Option 4: "Lucid" (स्पष्ट): Means clear and easy to understand; this is actually a near-synonym of "vivid", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Be careful: options like "Pictorial" and "Lucid" are deliberately placed near-synonyms (or related words) to "vivid" to mislead in an ANTONYM question — always check the exact opposite meaning, not just a related word.

• Other antonyms of "vivid": dull, faint, hazy, indistinct, blurred.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement required’.
The annual seed festival hosted in Auroville promote sharing of traditional knowledge and sustainable farming practices.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. promotes sharing of traditional.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The annual seed festival", a singular noun. In the Simple Present Tense, a singular subject (other than "I"/"you") requires the verb to take an "-s/-es" ending.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular Subject + V1 + s/es (in Simple Present Tense). Hence "festival" must take "promotes", not "promote".

◦ Example: The seed festival promotes sharing of traditional knowledge. (not "promote")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "promotes sharing of traditionally" is incorrect because "traditionally" is an adverb and cannot modify the noun "knowledge"; the sentence needs the adjective "traditional".

• Option 3: "promotes sharing of tradition" changes "traditional knowledge" (a specific type of knowledge) to "tradition knowledge", which is grammatically and idiomatically incorrect phrasing.

• Option 4: "No improvement required" is incorrect because the original sentence has a clear subject-verb agreement error ("festival promote"), which must be corrected.

NOTE

• Subject-verb agreement is one of the most frequently tested grammar rules in SSC exams — always identify the true grammatical subject (ignoring intervening phrases) before deciding singular/plural verb form.

• Do not confuse adjectives ending in common suffixes (e.g., "traditional") with their adverb forms ending in "-ly" (e.g., "traditionally") — check what part of speech the sentence requires (here, an adjective modifying "knowledge").

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Magnanimos.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "Magnanimous", meaning generous or forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful.

◦ Example: The winning captain was magnanimous in victory, praising the losing team's effort.

• Spelling key: MAGN + ANIM + OUS. The word ends in the adjective suffix "-ous", which is often mis-spelt as "-os" or "-us"; the given option "Magnanimos" wrongly drops this ending.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Accompanied" — correctly spelt; past tense of "accompany" (y changes to "i" before adding "-ed").

• Option 3: "Fascination" — correctly spelt; noun form of "fascinate", meaning a strong attraction or interest.

• Option 4: "Psychology" — correctly spelt; note the silent "p" at the start and the "-ch-" sound spelt with "ch".

NOTE

• Many English adjectives end in the suffix "-ous" (meaning "full of" or "having the quality of"): generous, famous, dangerous, courageous, magnanimous — always check this ending carefully in spelling questions.

• The opposite of "magnanimous" is "petty" or "mean-spirited".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Sacred
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Profane.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Sacred" means connected with God or a god; considered holy and deserving veneration/respect. (पवित्र)

• "Profane" means showing disrespect for God or holy things; not connected with religion or spirituality; secular, which is the direct opposite of "sacred". (अपवित्र)

◦ Example: The temple is a sacred place, whereas the marketplace outside is entirely profane/secular.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Grave" (गंभीर): Means "serious" (a grave situation) or "a burial place" (a noun); neither meaning is opposite to "sacred".

• Option 2: "Narrow" (संकीर्ण): Means "of small width" or, figuratively, "limited in outlook"; it is unrelated to the religious sense of "sacred".

• Option 3: "Holy" (पवित्र): This is actually a close synonym of "sacred", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Be careful of distractor options that are synonyms (like "Holy" here) placed among antonym choices — always confirm you are picking the truly opposite word.

• Other antonyms of "sacred": secular, unholy, worldly, blasphemous.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Judgment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Following the British spelling convention used in SSC examinations, the correct spelling is "Judgement" (with the letter "e" retained before "-ment"). The given option "Judgment" (without the "e") follows the American spelling convention and is treated as incorrect here.

◦ Example: The judge delivered her judgement after hearing both sides.

• Spelling key: JUDGE + MENT = JUDGEMENT (British). The silent "e" of "judge" is retained before adding the suffix "-ment" in British English, unlike in American English, which drops it.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Chief" — correctly spelt; remember the pattern "ie" as in "chief", "belief", "relief".

• Option 2: "Relevant" — correctly spelt; note the "-ant" ending, not "-ent".

• Option 3: "Colleague" — correctly spelt; note the "-eague" ending, from French "collègue".

NOTE

• Other British vs. American spelling differences frequently tested by SSC: colour/color, favour/favor, centre/center, organise/organize, programme/program.

• SSC's official answer key generally follows British spelling, so always prefer the British form when a spelling difference like "judgement/judgment" appears.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Alive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Dead.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Alive" means living, not dead; having life. (जीवित)

• "Dead" means no longer living, which is the direct and literal opposite of "alive". (मृत)

◦ Example: The old oak tree, once alive with birdsong, now stands dead and bare.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Wise" (बुद्धिमान): Means having good judgment/knowledge; unrelated to the state of being alive or dead.

• Option 2: "Animated" (जीवंत/सजीव): Means lively and full of energy; this is actually close in meaning to "alive" (a synonym in the figurative sense), not its opposite.

• Option 3: "Spry" (फ़ुर्तीला): Means active and energetic, especially for an old person; again, this is closer to "alive/lively" than to "dead".

NOTE

• Be careful of options that are actually synonyms (like "Animated" and "Spry" here) placed as distractors in ANTONYM questions.

• Other antonyms of "alive": lifeless, inanimate, deceased, defunct.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the following sentence.
You should never visit her without her consent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Refusal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Consent" means permission or agreement to do something. (सहमति/अनुमति)

• "Refusal" means the act of declining or saying no to something, which is the direct opposite of giving one's agreement/permission. (इनकार)

◦ Example: Despite her refusal, he went ahead without her consent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Approval" (स्वीकृति): Means official acceptance or agreement; this is actually a near-synonym of "consent", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Permission" (अनुमति): Also a near-synonym of "consent" (both mean allowing something to happen), not an antonym.

• Option 3: "Knowledge" (ज्ञान): Means awareness or information about something; it is unrelated to the idea of agreeing or disagreeing.

NOTE

• Be careful: two of the distractors here ("Approval", "Permission") are actually synonyms of "consent" — a common trap in ANTONYM questions.

• Other antonyms of "consent": denial, dissent, disagreement, objection.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.
He was the fastest between all the contestants.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. amongst.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Between vs. Among(st): "Between" is used when referring to exactly two people/things, while "Among/Amongst" is used when referring to more than two people/things.

• Since the sentence refers to "all the contestants" (clearly more than two), the correct preposition is "amongst" (or "among"), not "between".

◦ Example: He was the fastest amongst all the contestants. (not "between all the contestants")

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain a preposition error — "between" cannot be used for more than two entities.

• Option 2: "since" is a preposition of time (used with a specific point in time, e.g., "since 2020") and makes no grammatical or logical sense here.

• Option 4: "from" does not fit the meaning required (comparing one contestant's speed relative to a group), so it cannot correctly replace "between" here.

NOTE

• "Amongst" is a slightly more formal/archaic variant of "among"; both are correct, but "among" is more common in modern usage.

• Similar countable-based preposition pairs tested by SSC: "each other" (for two) vs. "one another" (for more than two).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
There is no place on the bench.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. no room.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The standard, idiomatic English expression for a lack of available space (for a person or object to fit) is "no room", not "no place". "Room" here is used as an uncountable noun meaning "available space".

• Rule — Fixed collocation: "There is no room for/on something" = there is not enough space. "Place" is not idiomatically used with "no" in this sense of physical space.

◦ Example: There is no room on the bench for another person to sit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "more space" changes the meaning of the sentence from a negative statement (no space) to claiming there is additional space, which contradicts the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "no life" is nonsensical in this context; "life" does not relate to physical space on a bench.

• Option 3: "more place" is both grammatically incorrect ("place" is not typically quantified with "more" in this sense) and changes the meaning, similar to option 1.

NOTE

• Distinguish between "room" (uncountable noun meaning "space", e.g., "no room to move") and "room" (countable noun meaning "a chamber in a building", e.g., "a bedroom").

• Similarly, "place" as a countable noun usually refers to a specific location or seat (e.g., "save my place"), not general available space.
